newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH CREDIT ACTION GROWS DESPITE HIGH RATES.
newsitem.headline: POLISH CREDIT ACTION GROWS DESPITE HIGH RATES.

text.p: Polish credit action remained rampant during the first quarter despite the central bank's tight monetary policy, which analysts said may put the brakes on any potential interest rate cuts for some time.

The National Bank of Poland (NBP) reported on Wednesday that credit action grew 2.9 percent in March and 8.5 percent since the start of the year, while broad money as a whole grew 2.2 percent last month and 4.1 percent in the first quarter.

Analysts said credit, especially the so-called consumption credit for households, continued to grow despite an increase of lending rates because Poles had confidence in future earnings and were not concerned with slightly higher loan payments.

"The average Pole, Mr. Kowalski doesn't care how much he pays for credit, but lending rates are essential for firms and this is why personal credit is growing quicker than corporate lending," said Andrzej Burliga, analyst at Bank Zachondni SA.
During the first quarter personal credit grew by 10 percent while corporate credit 8.3 percent, allthough lending to non-financials remained much higher in nominal terms.

Analysts said the credit boom, which started in late 1996, was caused by a fast growth of real wages along with easier access to credit financing, not readily available during the first years of transformation because of high inflation.
The fast rise of credit in March came as a surprise to many analysts, who expected credit growth to slow in line with an increase in obligatory reserves from the end of February.
In response to the increased costs stemming form the reserve requirement rise many commercial banks pushed up credit rates, but this did little to cool Poland's hungry consumers.
"The March credit growth is unsettling...and it certainly signals that the NBP should enforce a very tight monetary policy," said Krzysztof Bledowski, head economist at WoodCommerz in Warsaw.

Analysts, who earlier expected a reduction of official interest rates, now at 22 and 25 percent, in the third quarter, were now beginning to look for the next rate move to occur around the turn of the third and fourth quarters, if at all.
"Interest rates will remain at present levels, there is no reason to increase them and any cuts are not likely until at least the autumn," said Ewa Lipinska, analyst at PBK SA bank.

The central bank last week signalled that interest rates may fall in the longer term when it refrained to increase yields of 182-day and 273-day NBP-bills after earlier lifting yields on its 91-day paper and its reverse repo drainages.

Many analysts said that interest rates, last trimmed in July 1996 when inflation was year-on-year 20.4 percent, should be reduced along with falling annual price growth, which stood at 17.3 percent in February.

For the last four months the central bank has kept a tight monetary policy to cool credit action and domestic demand in order to keep a lid on consumer imports which could sharply widen Poland's current account deficit in the years to come.
